The fourth installment of Er Mu’s translation of Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking starts with a puzzle: adults hear up to 20,000 Hz, yet speech can be understood with everything below 4,000 Hz, which is why phone calls can get by with a narrow bandwidth. Why, then, did we keep such good high-frequency hearing? Rickye Heffner of the University of Toledo argues that high frequencies help us locate sounds, which we do by comparing the arrival time and level at our two ears.

Localization acuity does not simply follow head size: people can pinpoint a loudspeaker to within a degree or two, horses only to about 25°. After testing species from elephants to fruit bats, Heffner concluded that the ears’ job is to point the eyes. Horses, with a 180° field of view, need little acuity; humans, with a narrow field of best vision, need much more. Her chart of more than 30 species bears this out. Our asymmetric outer ears, which work at high frequencies, tell front from back. The oldest fossil outer ear belongs to Spinolestes, found in Spain in 2015, which lived 125 million years ago.

Finally, Rolf Quam’s team modeled early hominin hearing from CT scans. Australopithecus africanus and Paranthropus robustus were probably already slightly more sensitive at 1,500–3,000 Hz, long before language, and Homo heidelbergensis and Neanderthals heard much as we do. Speech, Cox concludes, sits in that band because our hearing is most sensitive there, not the other way around.

Translated into Chinese by Er Mu (edited by Er Mu and Fanyu Meng) from Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking: Human Conversation from the Neanderthals to Artificial Intelligence (2018). About the book.
